publication_scope.blurb: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu - Sedan Theological Theses, newly rendered from the 1675 London Latin. Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-LIX), and on the various distinctions and senses of grace in the Roman School (I-LXX) and in the Reformed Schools (I-XLIX), and on the Roman School's division of grace into sufficient and efficacious (I-CXLV, complete), and on the Protestant doctrine of that distinction, the Lutherans of the Augsburg Confession, the Remonstrants, and the Reformed who subscribe to Dort, with the Reformed debate on how grace moves the will, Le Blanc's concluding comparisons and an appendix on the Socinians (I-LXXXVIII, complete), and on whether and how far man can fulfil the Law by Christ's grace (I-LI, complete). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: XXXIV. Verum hic non opus est privatorum Doctorum testimonia recensere, cum quae sit in hac quaestione Ecclesiarum nostrarum sententia, publicis earum confessionibus & declarationibus, cuivis notum & compertum esse possit. Sic enim habet confessio Reformatorum in regno Poloniae quae fuit in Colloquio Thoruniensi oblata, cap. 4. sect. 2. part. 10. Falso, inquiunt, accusamur, quasi praecepta Christi nullomodo a fidelibus servari posse statuamus: Cum tamen illa, non quidem propriis viribus, sed per gratiam spiritus sancti, non tantum servari posse, sed etiam omnino servari ab omnibus debere doceamus. Et quidem non voto tantum, aut proposito inefficaci, sed etiam ipso opere, & vero, sincero, ac totius vitae perseveranti studio. Quamvis in hac vita non ita perfecte a quoquam serventur, aut servari possint, ut legi Dei satisfaciamus, eamque per omnia impleamus; sed ut simul & imperfectionis & infirmitatis propriae sensu, variorum lapsuum & delictorum veniam quotidie a Deo petere opus habeamus. Et eandem quoque doctrinam aliis verbis exprimit confessio Anglicana anni M.DC.XLV. c. 19. paragr. 7. ubi dicit spiritum Christi voluntatem hominis ita domare & flectere, ut alacriter ac cum voluptate faciat, id quod requirit Dei voluntas, in lege ejus revelata.
english: Thesis XXXIV. There is no need here to go through the testimonies of private doctors. Anyone can learn and confirm what our churches hold on this question from their public confessions and declarations.

The confession of the Reformed in the kingdom of Poland, presented at the Colloquy of Thorn (chapter 4, section 2, part 10), puts it this way: 'We are falsely accused of holding that the faithful cannot keep Christ's precepts in any way. We teach that they can be kept, not by our own strength but by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and more than that, that everyone is bound to keep them fully: not merely in wish or in a purpose that comes to nothing, but in actual deed, with a true, sincere zeal that lasts the whole of life.

In this life, however, no one keeps them so perfectly, or can, that we satisfy God's law and fulfil it in every respect. We still need, aware of our own imperfection and weakness, to ask God every day to pardon our many slips and offences.'

The English confession of 1645 states the same doctrine in other words in chapter 19, paragraph 7, where it says that Christ's Spirit so tames and bends the human will that it does readily and gladly what God's will, revealed in his law, requires.

source_text: XXXV. Ex his manifestum est Ecclesiae Reformatae Doctores non negare fideles per Christi gratiam aliquo modo, & sensu posse legem implere, & Dei mandata servare, veram, scilicet, iis praestando obedientiam. Itaque quum aliquando dicunt fidelibus ipsis impossibile esse implere Dei legem, & observare illius mandata, id juxta eorum mentem, exponendum est non de quavis impletione & observatione, sed de illa demum quae sit perfecta atque absoluta: quod diligenter monent, quum quaestionis hujus statum explicant. Tum enim observant omnes, cum Chemnitio, in Examine Sessionis sextae Concilii Tridentini, inter Pontificios & Protestantes non quaeri simpliciter, An lex per Dei gratiam impleri possit, sed an possit impleri perfecte. Cum inchoatam atque imperfectam ejus impletionem Renatis ultro concedant Protestantes.
english: Thesis XXXV. This makes it plain that the doctors of the Reformed Church do not deny that believers, by Christ's grace, can in some way and in some sense fulfil the law and keep God's commandments, that is, by giving them true obedience.

So when they sometimes say that it is impossible even for believers to fulfil God's law and observe its commandments, their meaning is not any fulfilment or observance at all, but only one that is perfect and absolute. They take care to point this out when they set out the state of the question.

At that point they all note, with Chemnitz in his Examen of the sixth session of the Council of Trent, that the question between the papists and the Protestants is not simply whether the law can be fulfilled by God's grace, but whether it can be fulfilled perfectly. For the Protestants readily grant the regenerate a begun and imperfect fulfilment of it.

source_text: XXXVI. Ex iis etiam quae allata sunt patet, quum Protestantes iidem, affirment legis divinae mandata a fidelibus servari inchoate, non absolute; imperfecte, non consummate: per id eos negare nolle quin obedientia illa quam legi praestant, integra atque sincera sit, & quin per eam toti legi divinae, & singulis ejus praeceptis se submittant: adeoque quin constituat justitiam talem quae Deo placeat & probetur, & quam Deus olim benigne sit remuneraturus: contra quam ipsis tribuere solent Ecclesiae Romanae Doctores. Proindeque Protestantes Renatorum obedientiae non denegare perfectionem illam, quam partium diximus, & ab ea solum removere, quam graduum appellant. Quae distinctio in hunc usum ab ipsis adhiberi solet, ut videre est apud Joannem Davenantium, de justitia actuali, cap. 51. Neque nos, inquit, unquam inficias ivimus posse Renatos, & spiritu charitatis imbutos, etiam hostes suos diligere, posse etiam caeteros actus facere qui mandantur in Decalogo. Sed in operibus hisce faciendis, assequuntur illam solummodo quam Theologi appellant perfectionem partium, non perfectionem graduum.
english: Thesis XXXVI. What has been cited also shows something else. When these same Protestants say that believers keep the commandments of the divine law in a begun way and not absolutely, imperfectly and not completely, they do not mean to deny that the obedience believers give the law is whole and sincere. Nor do they deny that by it believers submit to the whole divine law and to each of its precepts, so that it makes up a righteousness that pleases God, has his approval, and will one day be graciously rewarded by him. The doctors of the Roman Church usually charge them with denying this.

So Protestants do not refuse the obedience of the regenerate the perfection we have called perfection of parts; they deny it only the one called perfection of degrees. They regularly use the distinction for this purpose, as can be seen in John Davenant, on actual righteousness, chapter 51:

'We have never denied that the regenerate, filled with the spirit of love, can love even their enemies, and can perform the other acts the Decalogue commands. But in doing these works they reach only what theologians call perfection of parts, not perfection of degrees.'

source_text: XXXVII. Quibus consentanea sunt quae leguntur apud Paraeum in Bell. lib. 4. de Justif. cap. 11. pag. 1077. In locis allegatis, inquit, quae perfectionem aliquibus tribuunt, vel ab omnibus requirunt, perfectio intelligitur non graduum, sive is obedientiae gradus quem legis ἀκρίβεια, requirit, sed perfectio partium, sive integritas opposita hypocrisi, hoc est, verus & non simulatus affectus & studium obediendi Deo, & repugnandi cupiditatibus; atque initium obedientiae secundum omnia Dei mandata. Qua in re quoque vestigia Paraei premit Vendelinus, Christianae Theologiae lib. 1. cap. 26. in explicatione theseos 10. sect. 3. Perfectio, inquit, quae sanctis tribuitur non est graduum, sed partium, non est absoluta, sed limitata, quam sinceritatem appellamus. Verum merito posset videri superfluum hac de re Reformatorum citare testimonia: cum distinctio ista perfectionis in illum usum adhibita, tam frequens sit apud eos, ut pauci sint apud quos reperiri non possit.
english: Thesis XXXVII. This agrees with what we read in Pareus on Bellarmine's De justificatione, book 4, chapter 11, page 1077: 'In the passages cited, which ascribe perfection to some or require it of all, the perfection meant is not of degrees, the degree of obedience the law's exactness (ἀκρίβεια) requires, but perfection of parts: integrity as opposed to hypocrisy, that is, a true and unfeigned desire and zeal to obey God and to resist evil desires, and a beginning of obedience to all God's commandments.'

Wendelin follows in Pareus's footsteps on this point in his Christian Theology, book 1, chapter 26, explaining thesis 10, section 3: 'The perfection ascribed to the saints is not of degrees but of parts; it is not absolute but limited, and we call it sincerity.'
Indeed it might well seem pointless to cite Reformed testimonies on this matter. They use this distinction of perfection for that purpose so often that few of them lack it.

source_text: XXXVIII. Id solum igitur in hac quaestione Protestantes negare intendunt, fideles per Christi spiritum renovatos legem implere posse, secundum totam illam perfectionem, quam lex rigide sumpta, ab homine exigit. Porro lex rigide sumitur quum aestimatur ex prima sua institutione, & spectatur quatenus primo homini lata fuit, & continet primum illud foedus cum homine initum, ex cujus observatione perennem & beatam vitam, a Dei bonitate & justitia simul expectare debebat. Lex autem sic considerata exigebat ab homine perpetuam obedientiam, nullis peccatis interruptam, nec ullis defectibus, & naevis obscuratam, & per quam homo cum summa alacritate, absque ulla pugna, vel renitentia affectuum internorum, in omnibus omnino, sine exceptione, sese voluntati divinae submitteret. Qualem, scilicet, obedientiam primi nostri parentes, in statu innocentiae, Deo exhibere poterant, & exhibere reapse tenebantur, ut in beato illo statu manerent, & tandem aeterna cum Deo felicitate fruerentur.
english: Thesis XXXVIII. The one thing Protestants mean to deny in this question, then, is that believers renewed by Christ's Spirit can fulfil the law with the whole perfection that the law, strictly taken, demands of man.

The law is taken strictly when it is judged by its first institution: as it was given to the first man and contained the first covenant made with him, by keeping which he was to look for unending and blessed life from God's goodness and justice together.

Taken in that way, the law demanded of man a perpetual obedience, broken by no sins and darkened by no defects or flaws, in which he would submit himself to God's will with the utmost readiness, with no struggle or resistance of the inner affections, in absolutely everything and without exception. This was the obedience our first parents could give God in the state of innocence, and were actually bound to give, so that they might remain in that blessed state and at last enjoy eternal happiness with God.

source_text: XXXIX. Talem autem obedientiam jam a Christi fidelibus, quantumvis ampla spiritus ejus copia donatis, praestari non posse per se manifestum est. In omnibus enim illis caro luctatur adversus spiritum, & plures motus rectae rationi rebelles, adeoque legi divinae repugnantes, identidem excitat. Proindeque magnam ad male agendum pronitatem, & in bene agendo difficultatem non parvam in se experiuntur. Unde fit ut quotidie in multis offendant, juxta dictum Jacobi, & inter eos, vel nulli, vel rari sint, qui non etiam in gravia peccata quandoque labantur.
english: Thesis XXXIX. It is self-evident that Christ's faithful cannot now give such obedience, however richly he has endowed them with his Spirit. In all of them the flesh fights against the Spirit and again and again stirs up many impulses that rebel against right reason and so oppose the divine law.

They therefore find in themselves a strong bent toward doing evil and no small difficulty in doing good. As a result they stumble daily in many things, as James says, and there are few of them, if any, who do not at some time slip into grave sins as well.

source_text: XL. Rem vero ita se habere, neque fideles in hac naturae corruptione atque infirmitate, posse ad modo descriptam perfectionem assurgere, res est ipsa experientia, & communi fidelium sensu, ac interno conscientiae testimonio tam evidens, ut eam negare nec possint, nec ausint ipsi Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae: sed hac in parte cogantur veritati dare manus. Cujus rei fidem abunde facere potest vel unus Stapletonus, vir inter suos non parvae authoritatis, idemque acerrimus Protestantium hostis, ac Pontificiae doctrinae defensor, qui magno cum suorum applausu, libros integros duodecim scripsit de justificatione, & quaestionibus annexis, totumque librum sextum insumpsit in pertractanda praesenti quaestione de impletione legis. Atque ut istud clarius pateat, breviter hic in summam redigere visum est quae Doctor ille dicto libro prolixe edisserit.
english: Thesis XL. That this is so, and that believers in this corrupt and weak state of nature cannot rise to the perfection just described, is so plain from experience itself, from the common sense of believers and the inner witness of conscience, that the doctors of the Roman Church themselves neither can nor dare deny it. On this point they are forced to yield to the truth.

Stapleton alone is ample proof. He was a man of no small authority among his own, a fierce enemy of the Protestants and a defender of papal doctrine, who to the great applause of his party wrote twelve whole books on justification and related questions and gave the entire sixth book to the present question of fulfilling the law. To make this clearer, it seems right to summarize briefly here what that doctor sets out at length in that book.

source_text: XLI. Igitur cap. 2. postquam dixit, juxta Doctrinam Catholicam, certum esse homines justificatos, per bona opera quae in Deo fiunt, divinae legi, pro hujus vitae statu, plene satisfacere, hanc doctrinam explicat multis propositionibus, quarum haec est prima, quam illo capite probare contendit. Renovati & justificati in Christo gratiam Spiritus sancti accipiunt qua legem impleant. Cap. vero tertio haec est secunda ejus propositio. Haec tamen impletio legis non intelligitur necessario & precise in omnibus mandatis legis, toto tempore & cursu justitiae humanae: sed ille censetur implere legem, satisfacere legi, & in conspectu Dei justus habetur, qui voluntatem & affectum habens implendi universa legis praecepta, eatenus implet quatenus humana fragilitas, in reliquiis naturae corruptae per gratiam adjuta, implere in hac vita, vel potest, vel solet. Et postea ex eo quod scriptura affirmat, neminem in hac vita sine peccato esse, & tamen multos justos in omnibus Dei mandatis ambulasse testatur, colligit aliquem esse modum omnia mandata faciendi, sive totam legem implendi, quamvis universalis & omnimoda adimpletio non sit; Atque in fine capitis observat, longe aliud esse ad justitiam requiri ut universa lex ab homine justo, per totam ejus vitam, vel certe post primam ejus conversionem perpetuo adimpleatur, quod damnat ipse tanquam Pelagianum: aliud vero dicere justificatum in Christo posse aliqua bona opera facere, quae ita legem Dei impleant, seu legi satisfaciant, ut in conspectu & judicio Dei illa opera sint vere bona, laudabilia & justa, ipseque homo ea faciens vere propterea justus coram Deo habeatur: Quod orthodoxam esse sententiam asserit.
english: Thesis XLI. In chapter 2, then, having said that according to Catholic doctrine it is certain that justified people fully satisfy the divine law, as far as the condition of this life allows, by good works done in God, he unfolds this teaching in a series of propositions. The first, which he tries to prove in that chapter, is: 'The renewed and justified in Christ receive the grace of the Holy Spirit by which to fulfil the law.'

His second proposition, in chapter 3, is: 'This fulfilment of the law is not meant necessarily and strictly of every commandment of the law, throughout the whole time and course of human righteousness. A person is counted as fulfilling and satisfying the law, and is held righteous in God's sight, if he has the will and desire to fulfil all the precepts of the law and fulfils them as far as human frailty, aided by grace amid the remnants of corrupt nature, can or usually does fulfil them in this life.'

Later, because Scripture both says that no one in this life is without sin and testifies that many righteous people walked in all God's commandments, he concludes that there is a way of doing all the commandments, or fulfilling the whole law, even though it is not a universal and complete fulfilment.

At the end of the chapter he notes that it is one thing to require for righteousness that a righteous person fulfil the whole law perpetually through his whole life, or at least from his first conversion on, which he himself condemns as Pelagian. It is another to say that someone justified in Christ can do some good works that fulfil or satisfy God's law in such a way that, in God's sight and judgment, those works are truly good, praiseworthy and righteous, and the person who does them is truly held righteous before God on that account. This, he says, is the orthodox view.

source_text: XLII. Cap. 4. Tertia illius propositio sic habet. Qui mandata legis observat, utcunque in multis offendat, justus tamen coram Deo esse potest, si plures habet virtutes quam vitia. Circa quod observat neminem esse justum qui non plura habeat peccata venialia quam virtutum opera; sed hic comparari opera virtutum cum gravibus peccatis, quorum uni levia multa non aequiparantur: adeo ut sensus sit illum justum haberi qui post primam conversionem, in toto progressu justitiae suae, in toto cursu & conflictu praesentis vitae, plures habet praeclaras virtutes quam gravia & lethifera peccata: Vel qui multo frequentius magisque assidue pietatis & charitatis operibus incumbit, quam in grave aliquod flagitium delabitur: denique qui saepius vincit quam vincitur.
english: Thesis XLII. His third proposition, in chapter 4, reads: 'Someone who observes the commandments of the law, however much he stumbles in many things, can still be righteous before God if he has more virtues than vices.'

On this he remarks that no one is righteous who does not have more venial sins than works of virtue. Here, he says, works of virtue are being compared with grave sins, and many light sins do not equal a single grave one.

The meaning, then, is that a person counts as righteous who, after his first conversion, throughout the progress of his righteousness and the whole course and struggle of this present life, has more excellent virtues than grave and deadly sins; or who gives himself to works of piety and love far more often and more steadily than he falls into some grave crime; in short, who wins more often than he loses.

source_text: XLIII. Cap. 5. Docet mandatorum impletionem in hac vita talem non esse ut omni prorsus peccato careat: tamen talem & tantam esse ut gravibus illis & lethiferis peccatis omnino carere possit & debeat. Justos quidem ipsos etiam interdum lethaliter peccare: Verum in tali peccato constitutos justos non esse, neque legem implere: nec veram justitiam cum tali peccato, nondum per poenitentiam deleto, consistere, licet cum aliis levioribus peccatis, etiam quotidie commissis, vera hujus vitae justitia consistat.
english: Thesis XLIII. In chapter 5 he teaches that in this life the fulfilment of the commandments is not such as to be entirely free of all sin, but that it is such, and so great, that it can and must be entirely free of grave and deadly sins.

The righteous themselves, he grants, sometimes sin mortally. But while they are in such a sin they are not righteous and do not fulfil the law, and true righteousness cannot coexist with such a sin until repentance has blotted it out. The true righteousness of this life does coexist, however, with other, lighter sins, even those committed every day.

source_text: XLIV. Cap. 6. Haec est ejus quinta propositio, Justitia hujus vitae Evangelica, etsi non careat omni prorsus peccato, ideoque ex hac parte perfecta non sit; tamen suo modo perfecta est, quia id semper agit, ut careat peccato, proficiendo de die in diem. Explicat autem postea quo sensu dicat illam esse suo modo perfectam, nempe, quia vera justitia & vera obedientia est. Verum enim & plenum & perfectum hic pro eodem habet. Ac perfectum & plenum intelligit, cui nihil deest ad veram rationem & essentiam justitiae & obedientiae, ut pluribus indicat paragr. in hac ergo. & cap. 7. paragr. 1. Ubi dicit perfectam charitatem & justitiam dici quae vera est: quemadmodum perfectum odium dicitur illud quod est verum.
english: Thesis XLIV. His fifth proposition, in chapter 6, is: 'The evangelical righteousness of this life is not free of every sin whatever and is therefore not perfect in that respect; yet it is perfect in its own way, because it is always striving to be free of sin, advancing day by day.'

He then explains in what sense he calls it perfect in its own way: it is true righteousness and true obedience. Here he treats 'true', 'full' and 'perfect' as meaning the same thing, and by 'perfect' and 'full' he means that which lacks nothing needed for the true nature and essence of righteousness and obedience.

He shows this more fully in the paragraph beginning 'In hac ergo' and in chapter 7, paragraph 1, where he says that love and righteousness are called perfect when they are true, just as a hatred is called perfect when it is true.

source_text: XLV. Capitis septimi summam complectitur haec thesis, Quamvis justitia hujus vitae non sic adimpleat omnia mandata, quin saepius offendat, sitque potius in profectu quam in perfectione, id est perfecta operatione, aut possessione virtutum, tamen in eorum mandatorum quae facit justus observatione, seu adimpletione non peccat, utcunque mandatum ipsum perfectissime non impleat, quoad modum, seu gradum adimplendi. Et postea monet diligenter notandum, Catholicam Ecclesiam non docere perfectissimam mandatorum obedientiam esse ad justitiam & salutem necessariam: sed veram obedientiam, & hujusmodi qualem lex divina in hac vita a nobis exigit ut habeamus. Aliud enim est, inquit, vere & plene satisfacere legis mandato, ut illius, scilicet, transgressor non sis: sed illud vere & plene custodias, ita ut nec lex ipsa, nec Deus propter legem, quicquam in tuo opere juste damnet: aliud vero plenissime & perfectissime legi divinae satisfacere, ita sane ut nec lex, nec Deus propter legem quicquam in tuo opere amplius desideret. Illud enim in omni opere justo verum est. Istud in hac vita sititur & esuritur, non autem comprehenditur, non habetur.
english: Thesis XLV. The following thesis sums up chapter 7: 'Although the righteousness of this life does not fulfil all the commandments without often stumbling, and is in progress rather than in perfection, that is, rather than in perfect action or possession of the virtues, yet in observing or fulfilling the commandments he does keep, the righteous person does not sin, even if he does not fulfil the commandment itself most perfectly as to the manner or degree of fulfilling it.'

He then warns that it must be carefully noted that the Catholic Church does not teach that the most perfect obedience to the commandments is necessary for righteousness and salvation, but true obedience, the kind the divine law requires us to have in this life.

'It is one thing,' he says, 'to satisfy a commandment of the law truly and fully, so that you are not its transgressor but keep it truly and fully, with the result that neither the law itself nor God on account of the law can justly condemn anything in your work. It is another to satisfy the divine law most fully and most perfectly, so that neither the law nor God on account of the law looks for anything more in your work. The first holds true in every righteous work. The second is thirsted and hungered for in this life, but not attained or possessed.'

source_text: XLVI. Capite octavo probandam & illustrandam suscipit, septimam hanc propositionem. Justitia bonorum operum in fide est vera coram Deo justitia, utcunque mixta peccatis & imperfecta, tum quoad universa mandata implenda, tum quoad modum implendi, vereque & plane legi Dei satisfacit: non solum quia quam proxime accedit ad plenam & perfectam justitiam: aut quia gravioribus saltem criminibus caret: aut etiam quia id agit proficiendo de die in diem ut omni prorsus peccato careat, & plene satisfaciat: sed adhuc praeterea quia quicquid deest illi ad plenam & perfectam adimpletionem mandata praetermittendo, & frequenter venialiter peccando, sive propter imperfectionem in modo & ratione implendi, id totum Christi misericordia & gratia indulget atque ignoscit; facitque indulgendo ut perinde simus coram Deo justi, ac si universa ad amussim omnia mandata, eademque perfectissime fecissemus.
english: Thesis XLVI. In chapter 8 he sets out to prove and illustrate this seventh proposition: 'The righteousness of good works in faith is true righteousness before God, however much it is mixed with sins and imperfect, both as to the full range of commandments to be fulfilled and as to the manner of fulfilling them; and it truly and plainly satisfies God's law.

It does so not only because it comes as close as possible to full and perfect righteousness, or because it is at least free of the graver crimes, or even because it strives, advancing day by day, to be free of all sin and to satisfy the law fully.

It does so also because whatever it lacks for a full and perfect fulfilment, whether through leaving commandments undone and often sinning venially, or through imperfection in the manner and way of fulfilling, Christ's mercy and grace wholly overlooks and forgives; and by pardoning it, that mercy and grace makes us just as righteous before God as if we had done every one of the commandments exactly, and done them most perfectly.'

source_text: XLVII. Denique cap. 15. sic explicat quo sensu Renati legem impleant, & legi satisfaciant, ex sententia Ecclesiae Romanae. Nempe, inquit, quoties impleri legem a Renatis, vel Renatos plene satisfacere legi divinae docet Catholica Ecclesia, per verbum implendi, aut plene satisfaciendi intelligit illum implendi modum qui opponitur transgressioni legis: quae est aversio a tota latitudine legis, vel commissione, vel omissione facta, id est, veram mandatorum observationem & executionem intelligit. Non autem per verbum implendi, aut plene satisfaciendi intelligit plenam quasi mensuram modumque plenissimum, quo tota lex impleri possit, ut, videlicet, universa lex in tota sua latitudine semper & perfectissime observetur. Hoc enim ad plenam sanitatem & perfectam alterius vitae justitiam pertinet. Illud ad praesentis vitae certamen legitimum, cursumque rectum spectat. Quibus consequenter in eodem capite explicat quomodo justitia fidelium in hac vita certo respectu perfecta sit & non perfecta. Recolere, inquit, necesse est esse quidem nostram in hac vita justitiam aliquo sensu imperfectam: & inchoatam quandam esse in nobis novitatem: sed ideo imperfectam, quia non omni modo, & ex omni parte perfecta est: item ideo inchoatam, quia non est plena, qualis in altera vita erit: ubi tanta erit ut ei nihil addi queat: esse nihilominus pro capacitate hujus vitae, pro ratione justitiae praesentis, quae in conflictu, non in victoria, qua mors & lex peccati absorbentur, in stadio & cursu, non in bravio & praemio, denique in via, non in patria consistit, veri nominis justitiam.
english: Thesis XLVII. Finally, in chapter 15, he explains in what sense, according to the Roman Church, the regenerate fulfil and satisfy the law: 'Whenever the Catholic Church teaches that the law is fulfilled by the regenerate, or that the regenerate fully satisfy the divine law, by "fulfilling" or "fully satisfying" it means the kind of fulfilling that is the opposite of transgressing the law. Transgression is a turning away from the whole breadth of the law, by commission or by omission; so what it means is the true observance and carrying out of the commandments.

It does not mean by "fulfilling" or "fully satisfying" a full measure, as it were, and the fullest manner by which the whole law might be fulfilled, so that the entire law in all its breadth is kept always and most perfectly. That belongs to the full health and perfect righteousness of the next life; the other belongs to the lawful contest and right course of this present life.'

Following this, in the same chapter he explains how the righteousness of believers in this life is perfect in one respect and not perfect in another: 'We must remember that our righteousness in this life is indeed imperfect in some sense, and that the newness in us is only begun. It is imperfect because it is not perfect in every way and in every part; it is begun because it is not full, as it will be in the next life, where it will be so great that nothing can be added to it.

Even so, measured by the capacity of this life and by the nature of present righteousness, which lies in conflict, not in the victory in which death and the law of sin are swallowed up, in the race and the running, not in the prize and the reward, in short on the road and not in the homeland, it is a righteousness worthy of the name.'

source_text: XLVIII. His non absimilia reperiuntur apud Andradium celebrem quoque Scholae Romanae Theologum & non parvi nominis inter eos qui Concilio Tridentino interfuerunt. Nam in defensione fidei Tridentinae lib. 5. fol. 330. agnoscit legem coelestem quandam & angelicam integritatem & justitiam, ab omnique scelerum contagione maxime secretam & liberam, nobis praescribere, a qua Paulus ipse multum se distare fassus sit. Et postea subjungit, usurpans Augustini verba, Dei admirabilem legem ita hominum vitam instituere, affectionesque ita moderari, ut non modo officia praescribat quae deseri sine scelere non possint, sed illa etiam designet, quae expeti omni conatu debeant, quamvis a mortalibus carnis pondere pressis praestari perfecte nequeant. Quis enim, inquit, ita insaniet, ut omnes sese putet amoris numeros posse explere, quos Deus Opt. Max. illa oratione complexus est, Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, tota anima tua, & omnibus viribus tuis, cum ipsas intelligat felices mentes, quae omni solicitudine vacuae beatissimo numinis conspectu aevo sempiterno fruuntur, his amoris finibus nequaquam excedere? Verum cum absolutissimam amoris justitiaeque imaginem Deus voluisset mortalium oculis subjicere, non ea solummodo praescripsit, quae ab illis possent praestari, sed quae amore & desiderio essent prosequenda. Quo etiam omnia illa pertinent praecepta, quae nefariis cupiditatibus omnino interdicunt: nam quamvis illis prorsus carere mortales nequeant, in quibus vitiorum igniculi nondum consederunt, cupiditatibus tamen parere ita praeceptis illis prohibentur, ut simul quo omnia sunt piorum studia & cognitiones referendae plane demonstrent.
english: Thesis XLVIII. Much the same is found in Andrada, another celebrated theologian of the Roman school and a man of some standing among those who attended the Council of Trent. In his Defence of the Tridentine faith, book 5, folio 330, he acknowledges that the law prescribes for us a heavenly and angelic integrity and righteousness, wholly set apart and free from any taint of wrongdoing, from which Paul himself confessed he was far removed.

He then adds, in Augustine's words, that God's admirable law so orders human life and so governs our affections that it not only prescribes duties that cannot be neglected without wrongdoing, but also points to things that must be pursued with every effort, even though mortals weighed down by the flesh cannot achieve them perfectly.

'Who,' he says, 'would be so mad as to think he can fill up every measure of love that God, best and greatest, included in the command "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your strength", when he knows that even the blessed minds, free of every care and enjoying the most blessed sight of the Godhead for all eternity, never go beyond these bounds of love?

Since God wished to set before mortal eyes the most complete image of love and righteousness, he prescribed not only what they could achieve but also what they were to pursue with love and longing. All the precepts that flatly forbid wicked desires belong here too. Mortals, in whom the sparks of vice have not yet died down, cannot be wholly free of such desires; but those precepts forbid them to obey their desires in such a way as to show plainly, at the same time, the goal toward which all the efforts and thoughts of the godly must be directed.'

source_text: XLIX. Eadem de fidelium in hac vita imperfectione circa legem implendam, ex Augustino quoque, docet Ruardus Tapperus Professor Lovaniensis, in defensione articuli secundi pag. 76. Ubi affirmat, post sanctum illum Doctorem, esse quidem hic sanitatem, novitatem & justitiam, sed non plenam, nec perfectam, nisi modo quodam: sicut non hic est plena dilectio. Et legem, cujus plenitudo dilectio est, tunc demum ita implendam ut nihil omnino desit, quum dilectio Dei perfecta erit. Dei vero dilectionem non futuram esse perfectam antequam Deum videamus.
english: Thesis XLIX. Ruard Tapper, professor at Louvain, teaches the same about the imperfection of believers in this life with respect to fulfilling the law, drawing on Augustine as well, in his defence of the second article, page 76.

Following that holy doctor, he says that health, newness and righteousness do exist here, but not in full and not perfectly, except in a certain way, just as love is not full here. The law, whose fulfilment is love, will be fulfilled so completely that nothing at all is missing only when love for God is perfect; and love for God will not be perfect until we see God.

source_text: L. Denique cum obedientiam, quam fideles per Christi gratiam legi praestant, eo maxime nomine imperfectam esse censeant Protestantes, quod & quotidianae incursionis peccatis, quae venialia vocant Pontificii, assidue obscuretur, & gravioribus quoque, quae mortalia dicunt, non raro interrumpatur, utrumque hoc agnoscunt & supponunt ipsa Concilia Ecclesiae Romanae, & nominatim Tridentinum. Nam Sessione sexta, cap. undecimo, affirmat omnes in hac mortali vita, quantumvis sancti & justi sint, in levia saltem & quotidiana peccata, quae venialia dicuntur, quandoque cadere. Et in eadem Sessione Canone 23. anathema dicit eis qui docent hominem semel justificatum posse in tota vita omnia peccata, etiam venialia, vitare, nisi ex speciali Dei privilegio. Sessione vero 14. cap. 5. probat & confirmat constitutionem Concilii Lateranensis, per quam jubentur omnes & singuli fideles, posteaquam ad annos discretionis pervenerunt, saltem semel in anno, peccata sua confiteri sacerdoti: cum tamen idem Concilium, in eodem capite doceat non esse necessarium peccata venialia confiteri, sed mortalia tantum. Unde manifeste patet Concilium istud supponere omnes & singulos fideles, non solere annum integrum emetiri, quin grave aliquod peccatum admittant, quod non nisi per solennem poenitentiam expiari possit.
english: Thesis L. Finally, the chief reason Protestants judge the obedience believers give the law by Christ's grace to be imperfect is that it is constantly clouded by the sins of daily occurrence, which the papists call venial, and often interrupted by graver ones, which they call mortal. The councils of the Roman Church themselves, and Trent by name, acknowledge and presuppose both.

In session 6, chapter 11, Trent states that all people in this mortal life, however holy and righteous, fall at times into at least light and daily sins, the ones called venial. In canon 23 of the same session it anathematizes those who teach that a person once justified can avoid all sins, even venial ones, throughout his whole life, except by a special privilege from God.

In session 14, chapter 5, it approves and confirms the decree of the Lateran Council requiring each and every believer who has reached the age of discretion to confess his sins to a priest at least once a year, while the same council teaches in that chapter that venial sins need not be confessed, only mortal ones. Clearly, then, the council assumes that each and every believer does not usually get through a whole year without committing some grave sin that can be expiated only by solemn penance.

source_text: LI. Ex quibus omnibus colligere promptum est in obedientia quam Renati per Christi gratiam legi praestant, Protestantes ultro agnoscere perfectionem illam essentialem, quae consistit, in ejus veritate & sinceritate, pro qua pugnant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae. Et vicissim Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, quum dicunt fideles legem perfecte adimplere posse, per id tamen eorum obedientiae tribuere non velle perfectionem quae graduum dicitur, quam Protestantes ab ea removent, & quae consistit in exactissima & absolutissima conformitate cum lege, considerata juxta rigorem illum, secundum quem observari poterat & debebat ab homine, quum primum a Deo creatus est. Proindeque Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae immerito traducunt Ecclesiarum nostrarum hac in parte doctrinam, quasi tolleret gratiae Christi efficaciam, & pietatis studium in fidelibus multum imminueret, cum revera nihil hic doceant Protestantes, quod ipsi Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, juxta propria placita, fateri non cogantur.
english: Thesis LI. From all this it is easy to conclude, first, that in the obedience the regenerate give the law by Christ's grace, Protestants readily acknowledge the essential perfection the doctors of the Roman Church contend for, the perfection that consists in its being true and sincere.

Second, that the doctors of the Roman Church, when they say believers can fulfil the law perfectly, do not on that account mean to ascribe to their obedience the perfection called perfection of degrees, which Protestants deny it. That perfection consists in the most exact and absolute conformity with the law, taken in the strictness with which man could and had to keep it when God first created him.

So the doctors of the Roman Church have no ground for misrepresenting our churches' teaching on this point, as though it took away the power of Christ's grace and greatly weakened believers' zeal for godliness. In reality Protestants teach nothing here that the Roman doctors themselves are not forced to admit on their own principles.
